speaker: Zoltan Pozsar
title: Zoltan Pozsar on His Next Big Move and the Coming Monetary Divorce
question: In credit markets, why are corporate and commercial real estate losses generally less systemically dangerous when held by non-bank lenders rather than commercial banks?
guest: Credit and commercial real estate still have to go through their reckoning, but it's better to suffer those losses in non-banks than in banks. Banking crises are very nasty things, whereas if these losses get booked and absorbed on balance sheets that—I don't want to say aren't levered, because they are—but where that leverage doesn't really have much to do with money markets, that's orders of magnitude better to deal with than concentrated exposures inside the banking system. The general understanding about shadow banking these days is that anything happening outside a bank involving credit is shadow banking. That's not true to me, because true shadow banking is money-market funding of capital-market lending—you have to have a very strong money-market component, which is what actually amplifies things.

points.core: Non-bank credit funds absorb losses without relying on runnable money-market funding.
points.note: Accept: private credit or non-bank leverage being detached from short-term money markets or overnight funding, unlike deposit-funded banks. Do not credit: claiming non-bank lenders use zero leverage.

points.core: Systemic crisis amplification requires short-term money-market funding behind capital-market lending.
points.note: Accept: shadow banking defined mechanically as money-market funding of capital-market lending, where runnable short-term liabilities amplify shocks. Do not credit: defining shadow banking simply as any lending outside regulated banks.

points.core: Absorbing credit losses on non-bank balance sheets avoids concentrated systemic banking crises.
points.note: Accept: booking corporate or CRE losses in non-bank vehicles is far less destructive than concentrating them on commercial bank balance sheets. Do not credit: generic claims that non-banks are unregulated so they fail quietly.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main reason is the funding structure. Commercial banks finance long-term, illiquid loans with highly leveraged, short-term, runnable deposits, so losses can quickly erode thin capital, trigger depositor runs, and force fire sales. Because banks also run the payments system and provide credit to households and small businesses, their distress spreads broadly into the real economy and often requires government backstops such as deposit insurance and central bank lending.

Non-bank lenders such as private credit funds, insurers, pension funds, and mortgage REITs typically hold these loans with much less leverage and with long-dated, locked-up capital. Investors in closed-end funds cannot demand their money back on short notice, so losses are absorbed gradually by equity-like investors rather than causing a run. Their funding maturity matches their assets more closely, they play no role in payments, and their failure does not put insured deposits or taxpayers directly at risk.

The caveat is that this protection is not absolute: non-banks often borrow from banks, some vehicles offer redemption rights, and opacity can hide leverage, so risk can still flow back into the banking system.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Corporate and commercial real estate losses pose lower systemic risk at non-bank lenders primarily due to differences in funding stability, leverage, and economic centrality. Commercial banks engage in maturity transformation, funding illiquid, long-term loans with short-term, runnable deposits. When credit losses erode a bank’s relatively thin equity buffer, depositors and wholesale creditors may flee, triggering runs, forced asset fire sales, and broader financial contagion. Because banks also underpin the core payment system and supply essential working capital to households and businesses, their distress rapidly chokes off economic activity and threatens public safety nets like deposit insurance.

By contrast, non-bank lenders, such as private credit funds, insurers, and pension funds, typically finance loans with locked-up investor capital or long-duration liabilities matched to asset maturities. Operating with significantly lower leverage and minimal run risk, they rarely face sudden, forced liquidations. Credit losses are instead absorbed directly by end investors without disrupting payments or sparking systemic crises, provided bank lending to those non-banks remains contained.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main reason is how the money is funded. Banks use a lot of leverage and pay for their loans with short-term deposits that can be withdrawn at any moment. They also sit at the center of the payments system and of credit to households and businesses. When corporate or commercial real estate loans go bad at a bank, its thin equity cushion shrinks. That can set off depositor runs, fire sales and a pullback in lending to the whole economy, and governments may have to step in with deposit insurance or emergency funding.

Most non-bank lenders, such as private credit funds, insurers and pension funds, are funded by long-term, locked-up investor money and use modest leverage. Their investors are institutions that knowingly accepted the risk of losses. They generally can't run, so losses simply reduce returns for the people who signed up for them. These lenders don't take insured deposits or run payment systems, so their losses don't directly spread to the money supply or to taxpayers.

There are caveats. Risk can come back to banks through their loans to non-bank lenders, through hidden leverage, or through redemption pressure at semi-liquid funds. So non-bank lending is less dangerous, not risk-free.

Corporate and commercial real estate losses are generally less systemically dangerous at non-bank lenders because of how those institutions are funded, levered, and connected to the broader economy. Commercial banks finance illiquid, long-term loans with short-term, demandable deposits and operate with high leverage. When credit losses erode a bank's thin equity cushion, depositors can run, forcing fire sales of assets and threatening solvency. Because banks sit at the center of the payment system and interbank lending networks, distress at major banks can quickly freeze credit and transactions across the entire economy.

By contrast, non-bank lenders such as private credit funds, insurers, and pension funds typically rely on long-term, locked-up capital and use far less leverage. When loans sour, losses are absorbed directly by equity investors rather than triggering sudden redemptions, fire sales, or taxpayer-backed deposit insurance claims. While systemic risks can still resurface indirectly if banks lend heavily to these non-bank funds, keeping credit losses outside the deposit-taking core generally contains contagion.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol

Corporate and commercial real estate losses are generally less systemically dangerous when they fall on non-bank lenders funded by long-term investor capital. In a closed-end private credit fund, for example, loan losses reduce investors’ returns, but investors generally cannot withdraw their money on demand. That gives the fund time to work out troubled loans without selling assets into a falling market.

Commercial banks typically fund part of their long-term lending with deposits that can be withdrawn quickly. Loan losses erode bank capital, and if they shake depositor confidence, withdrawals can force asset sales that deepen losses and spread stress to other institutions. Banks may also cut lending to preserve capital, transmitting the shock to households and businesses.

The distinction depends on funding and leverage. Non-bank lenders that rely heavily on short-term borrowing, offer quick redemptions, or have substantial ties to banks can transmit stress through many of the same channels.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Commercial banks fund long-term loans partly with deposits that customers can withdraw on demand. Corporate or commercial real estate losses can erode a bank’s capital and shake depositors’ confidence. If depositors pull their money, the bank may have to sell assets quickly and cut lending. That can push asset prices down, squeeze otherwise healthy borrowers, and spread stress to other banks that provide credit and payment services.

Many non-bank lenders, such as closed-end private credit funds, rely on investor capital committed for years. They can often hold troubled loans through a workout, with investors absorbing the losses over time. The same loan loss is therefore less likely to trigger a run or a sharp contraction in credit across the economy. That advantage shrinks when non-bank lenders use heavy leverage, promise quick redemptions, or borrow heavily from banks.
